beats.trigger: ## Agents Building Agents (The Flywheel)
beats.got: nothing new; this is a title.

beats.trigger: The tool that builds tools compounds.
beats.got: The tool gets better by making more tools. I don't know what that means for people.

beats.trigger: Revisit the crux, what would have to be true, pre-mortem.
beats.got: There are three terms from earlier modules that I'd need to look up again.

beats.trigger: **Produce** a strategy kernel, suggested agent set, and two-week plan from your files
beats.got: The outputs are a strategy, a set of agents and a plan. That sounds closer to my world than the tool tricks did.

beats.trigger: The question to carry through: where is all this going?
beats.got: We work in a shared folder, and I wonder what ends up in it. I like the question, but nobody has said who is in the room.

beats.trigger: **Agent generates agent.** You watch one agent build another on real input.
beats.got: One agent builds another. It's short and I'm curious, but I'd like to know who owns the second one.

beats.trigger: You describe an agent; the coding agent builds it.
beats.got: I describe what I need and it builds it. The new-perspective option, a skeptic, is the one I'd pick.

beats.trigger: The job: *"On Mondays I need to Y; today I Z by hand."*
beats.got: Writing down the gap and the job is something I can do. It would be my weekly people-metrics summary.

beats.trigger: [You paste prompt "extend-your-system-1" into Claude and it works on it.]
beats.got: Claude built an agent from my four lines. I want to know whether it touched employee data, and nobody has asked.

beats.trigger: *"You used training data on line 4. Replace it or remove it."*
beats.got: I can push back on the output in plain words. That's a skill my HR business partners could learn.

beats.trigger: Monday's new gap gets a new agent in 25 minutes, not a new sprint.
beats.got: The next agent is quicker to build. The speed is the only reason given, and it doesn't tell me who learns this or who is afraid of it.

beats.trigger: **Time:** 70 minutes, in nine timed stages.
beats.got: There are nine stages, six files per agent and twenty agents. That's a lot of structure to hold in my head.

beats.trigger: Before you publish your context-manifest, redact customer names, partner-NDA material, M&A speculation and salary references.
beats.got: Other agents read what I publish, so I must redact salary and personal data first. In my company I would ask the DPO before this.

beats.trigger: Do not read other participants' stances yet: different context, sources, and judgment make the first round useful.
beats.got: We think alone first so the views differ. That's a sensible rule, and it works the same way in a leadership team.

beats.trigger: Find what your stance missed.
beats.got: The agent reads neighbours' stances and finds the gaps in mine. It's a third technical step in a row with no word about people.

beats.trigger: The file history shows who changed their mind and why.
beats.got: The file history records who changed their mind. I liked that. It also sounds like surveillance if you point it at people.

beats.trigger: Do not average the room.
beats.got: A central agent chooses between proposals. I zoned out because the page was mostly prompt text.

beats.trigger: The central synthesizer publishes operating instructions in the shared folder.
beats.got: The synthesizer's file steers everyone's agents midway. 'Injection' is a jargon word and is not explained.

beats.trigger: The selection board is the candidate, not final.
beats.got: Every agent criticizes the choice and can propose something better. The idea is good, but it was the fifth technical step in a row.

beats.trigger: The human picks.
beats.got: Agents do the work, but a person decides what to test next. That is the first thing that sounds like my answer on headcount.

beats.trigger: Close the session with three files at the shared folder root:
beats.got: The output is three files: kernel, agent set, plan.

beats.trigger: **Experiments.** Two or three assumptions to test: owner, experiment, success signal.
beats.got: The kernel names an owner and a success signal for each experiment. I could take that format to my leadership team.

beats.trigger: *"You are now agent builders.
beats.got: A sponsor tells the room it's now agent builders. That's a big claim, and I'd want proof before I said it to my people.

beats.trigger: The forum didn't converge on the first try. Pushback rounds were the work.
beats.got: Pushback rounds were the work, which I believe. It matches how change negotiations go.

beats.trigger: Four observations and two questions follow.
beats.got: After the exercises, the lecture finally steps back to meaning.

beats.trigger: What changed is who assembles them, and specifying well is the harder half.
beats.got: The skill that matters is specifying well. That is a people skill I can name, and my team can learn it.

beats.trigger: Access was instant and complete. What the room took up from each other is the smaller number.
beats.got: Access is not uptake. Giving everyone the tool doesn't mean they use each other's work, and I can take that to the leadership team.

beats.trigger: Without that rule, agents reading agents invent each other's sources
beats.got: Agents must cite files or they make up sources. It's a rule I can understand and check.

beats.trigger: The plan names the wall your company hits first: data access, runtime platform, or discoverability.
beats.got: Data access is the wall I'd hit first. That is my works council and DPO problem.

beats.trigger: The assembly is the durable half, and the assembly is what you spent your time on.
beats.got: Models change, and how you assemble the parts lasts.

beats.trigger: Nobody in this room knows yet, and the people running this training do not know either.
beats.got: The trainers admit they don't know what will be obsolete. That kind of understatement builds credibility with me.

beats.trigger: What your company knows about its own work gets better only when somebody writes it down and somebody else picks it up.
beats.got: The question is whether the organisation learns, and that is an HR question about how a skill spreads from one person to a team.

beats.trigger: If nobody can answer, you have a belief with a schedule attached.
beats.got: I can ask the leadership team what would make us drop our headcount assumption.

beats.trigger: Nothing in the room checked it. Hold that doubt as you did then.
beats.got: Nothing checked the result, so keep the doubt. I appreciate the honesty.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews the session, rewrites the most load-bearing file in place
beats.got: The agent reviews the session and rewrites a file. I'm not clear which file I would choose.

beats.trigger: The agent audits itself, so the summary is not neutral.
beats.got: The agent's summary of itself isn't neutral, so I should push back on it. I find that easy to trust.

beats.trigger: Agents must cite each other's files, or they invent what they never read.
beats.got: The recap is clear, but none of it is about roles or hiring.

beats.trigger: The agent that matters in six months is one nobody in this room has thought of.
beats.got: The most useful agent is one nobody has thought of yet, so the thing to build is the ability to make it.

take_homes: Having access to everyone's work is not the same as using it. Count what was actually taken up before promising a board a number.
Ask the leadership team what would make us drop a plan, so a belief doesn't just run on a schedule.
Agents do the work and a person decides what to test next. Specifying well is the skill to teach.

monday.move: Describe the weekly people-metrics summary agent in four lines (gap, job, what it reads, what it writes) and show it to one HR business partner, without real employee data.
monday.who: Me and one HR business partner
monday.stop_condition: If it needs real employee data, I stop and ask the DPO and the works council first.
monday.blocker: Employee data in an AI tool needs the works council and the DPO, and I haven't asked yet. This module never mentioned it.

misconception.why: The module never addressed headcount or which roles go. The 'organisation learns faster than the model' idea makes me ask what the real question is. I still expect headcount to be the first thing asked.

one_line: Good on the point that access isn't uptake and that a person still decides, but too many technical steps in a row and not a word on roles, hiring or works councils.
